      url: "https://eprints.maths.manchester.ac.uk/1217/1/paper9.pdf"
    - title: "Jan Zur, Matrix Functions, TU Berlin full lecture notes"
      url: "https://www.tu.berlin/fileadmin/www/40000110/Dauer-Wimis/Jan_Zur/matrix_functions_zur.pdf"

## Statement

If [[alg-pade-denominator-solve-by-householder-qr]] returns
verified-solution with output $X$ for exact complex matrices $M,C$ in its declared exact-controller model, then
$MX=C$ exactly. If $M$ is invertible, this solution is unique; in particular,
when used with an invertible Padé denominator, it is the exact denominator solve. This includes the original rational-input
instance and its finite exact rational audit whenever the adapter encodings
are supplied.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Exact complex matrices $M,C$ and a verified-solution output $X$.

[F1] The algorithm returns verified-solution only after exact controller
evaluation of $MX-C$ gives the zero matrix
([[alg-pade-denominator-solve-by-householder-qr]]).

[F2] The Padé numerator and denominator are $p_m(z)$ and
$q_m(z)=p_m(-z)$, and $r_m=p_m/q_m$ where the denominator is nonzero
([[def-diagonal-pade-approximant-for-exponential]]).

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], the exact residual $MX-C$ is zero, so the returned matrix satisfies $MX=C$. [given, F1]

2.1 If $M$ is invertible, left multiplication by $M^{-1}$ gives $X=M^{-1}C$, which is the unique solution. In the Padé use, take $M=Q_m(B)=q_m(B)$ and $C=P_m(B)=p_m(B)$ by [F2]; the conclusion applies whenever this denominator matrix is invertible. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

id: thm-matrix-function-rational-contour-error-bound
kind: theorem
title: "A resolvent contour bound transfers scalar rational error to matrices"
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: numerical-optimization-dynamics-2026-10-16
dependency_level: 4
deps:

  - lem-complex-infinity-matrix-norm-submultiplicative
  - def-complex-contours-reversal-concatenation-and-closedness
proof_strategy: direct
provenance:

verification:

sources:

    - title: "Jan Zur, Matrix Functions, TU Berlin full lecture notes"
      url: "https://www.tu.berlin/fileadmin/www/40000110/Dauer-Wimis/Jan_Zur/matrix_functions_zur.pdf"
    - title: "Nicholas J. Higham, Functions of Matrices, Handbook of Linear Algebra, Chapter 17"
      url: "https://eprints.maths.manchester.ac.uk/2109/1/fm2_final_njh.pdf"
---

## Statement

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, let $f$ be holomorphic on an open
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ containing $\sigma(A)$, and let $r$ be rational
with no pole on $\Omega$. Let $\Gamma$ be an admissible Cauchy cycle for $A$
contained in $\Omega$. Write its finite chain representation as $\Gamma=\sum_\nu m_\nu\gamma_\nu$ with integer coefficients and define its coefficient-weighted length by $L_\Gamma:=\sum_\nu|m_\nu|L(\gamma_\nu)$. The integral and this length use the same signed-chain representation. Suppose
$$\sup_{z\in\Gamma}|f(z)-r(z)|\le\varepsilon,\qquad \sup_{z\in\Gamma}\|(zI-A)^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le M.$$
Then
$$\|f(A)-r(A)\|_{\infty,\mathbb C} \le \frac{L_\Gamma}{2\pi}\,\varepsilon M.$$
The resolvent hypothesis may be supplied by the diskwise certificate of
[[thm-complex-resolvent-cover-certificate-soundness]]. A scalar disk error
alone does not give this matrix bound for a nonnormal matrix.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $A,f,r,\Omega,\Gamma,L_\Gamma,\varepsilon,M$ as in the statement.

[F1] Analytic primary matrix functions have the Cauchy-cycle representation
([[thm-analytic-primary-matrix-function-jordan-contour-agreement]]).

[F2] The complex infinity matrix norm is the maximum absolute row sum
([[def-complex-infinity-matrix-norm]]) and is submultiplicative
([[lem-complex-infinity-matrix-norm-submultiplicative]]).

[F3] The resolvent certificate gives the stated uniform bound on the supplied
contour when its disk inequalities hold
([[thm-complex-resolvent-cover-certificate-soundness]]).

## Proof

1.1 Since $f$ and $r$ are holomorphic on $\Omega$, [F1] applied to each gives $f(A)-r(A)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma (f(z)-r(z))(zI-A)^{-1}\,dz.$ The cycle is disjoint from $\sigma(A)$, so every resolvent in the integrand exists. [given, F1]

1.2 Write the finite chain integral as $\sum_\nu m_\nu\int_{\gamma_\nu}G$. Parametrize each rectifiable contour piece by arc length. Multiplying its estimate by $|m_\nu|$ and applying the triangle inequality to the finite chain sum gives the coefficient-weighted total $\sum_\nu|m_\nu|L(\gamma_\nu)=L_\Gamma$, including zero or negative coefficients. For every row, the absolute value of the integral is at most the integral of the absolute value; summing the row bounds and using [F2] gives $\left\|\int_\Gamma G(z)\,dz\right\|_{\infty,\mathbb C} \le L_\Gamma\sup_{z\in\Gamma}\|G(z)\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}.$ For $G(z)=(f(z)-r(z))(zI-A)^{-1}$, the hypotheses give $\sup_\Gamma\|G(z)\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le\varepsilon M$, with the resolvent bound certified by [F3]. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Taking norms in step 1.1, applying step 1.2, and using $|1/(2\pi i)|=1/(2\pi)$ proves the claimed estimate. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

id: alg-schur-parlett-matrix-function
kind: algorithm
title: "Finite Schur–Parlett recurrence with block merging and inconclusive statuses"
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: numerical-optimization-dynamics-2026-10-16
dependency_level: 7
deps:
  - def-analytic-primary-matrix-function
  - alg-exact-jordan-block-analytic-evaluation
  - thm-exact-jordan-block-analytic-evaluation-correct
  - def-real-and-complex-schur-forms
  - alg-finite-budget-francis-schur-reduction
  - def-sylvester-operator-and-separation-number
  - thm-sylvester-unique-solvability-spectral-separation
  - alg-bartels-stewart-sylvester-equation
  - thm-bartels-stewart-sylvester-exact-correctness
provenance:
  statement: literature-derived
  proof: not-applicable
verification:
  precheck: n/a
sources:
  references:
    - title: "Jan Zur, Matrix Functions, TU Berlin full lecture notes"
      url: "https://www.tu.berlin/fileadmin/www/40000110/Dauer-Wimis/Jan_Zur/matrix_functions_zur.pdf"
    - title: "Philip I. Davies and Nicholas J. Higham, A Schur–Parlett Algorithm for Computing Matrix Functions"
      url: "https://eprints.maths.manchester.ac.uk/156/1/paper.pdf"
---

## Definition

Input a finite complex matrix $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, a
holomorphic function $f$ on a neighborhood of $\sigma(A)$ with the finite
derivative data required by the diagonal block evaluators, Schur controls, a
Sylvester separation threshold $\tau\ge0$, an initial partition of
$\{1,\ldots,n\}$ into nonempty contiguous intervals, and a finite table of
exact Jordan certificates indexed by contiguous diagonal block intervals.
The partition and certificates are supplied inputs; a missing certificate for
any current block returns missing-jordan-data.

1. Call [[alg-finite-budget-francis-schur-reduction]] in its complex branch.
   Propagate any non-Schur status. Treat its returned $Q,T$ as candidates.
2. Verify by exact arithmetic that $Q^*Q=I$, $A=QTQ^*$, and $T$ is upper
   triangular. If any identity fails, return schur-certificate-failure. The
   computed Schur routine's residual diagnostic alone does not pass this test.
3. Start from the supplied contiguous block partition of $T$. For each block
   $T_{ii}$ call [[alg-exact-jordan-block-analytic-evaluation]] with its exact
   Jordan certificate and return value $F_{ii}$. If a certificate or required
   derivative is missing, return missing-jordan-data.
4. Visit block pairs by increasing distance $j-i$. Form
   $$C_{ij}=F_{ii}T_{ij}-T_{ij}F_{jj} +\sum_{i<k<j}(F_{ik}T_{kj}-T_{ik}F_{kj}).$$
   Call [[alg-bartels-stewart-sylvester-equation]] on
   $T_{ii}F_{ij}+F_{ij}(-T_{jj})=C_{ij}$ with threshold $\tau$. If it returns
   `success`, store its exact solution as $F_{ij}$. If it returns `singular-pivot` or
   `pivot-separation-failure` and the partition has multiple blocks, merge the
   contiguous blocks from $i$ through $j$, discard their old diagonal data,
   and restart step 3. Each merge reduces the block count, so there are at most
   $n-1$ merges. Any other non-success status is returned as
   inconclusive-sylvester with its underlying status.
5. Return the factored value $QFQ^*$ with status parlett-success.

The procedure makes no floating-point stability or error-bound claim. Its
success branch requires exact Schur and local solve certificates.

kind: theorem
title: "Separated Schur–Parlett blocks reconstruct the analytic matrix function"
status: draft
origin: pipeline

dependency_level: 8

proof_strategy: direct
provenance:

verification:

sources:
  references:
    - title: "Jan Zur, Matrix Functions, TU Berlin full lecture notes"
      url: "https://www.tu.berlin/fileadmin/www/40000110/Dauer-Wimis/Jan_Zur/matrix_functions_zur.pdf"
    - title: "Philip I. Davies and Nicholas J. Higham, A Schur–Parlett Algorithm for Computing Matrix Functions"
      url: "https://eprints.maths.manchester.ac.uk/156/1/paper.pdf"
---

## Statement

If [[alg-schur-parlett-matrix-function]] returns parlett-success for an exact
Schur pair $A=QTQ^*$, then its returned factored matrix $QFQ^*$ equals the
analytic primary matrix function $f(A)$. This is a conditional exact
correctness result, not a stability bound for the rounded Schur candidate
generation.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A successful algorithm output, its exact Schur certificate, its
diagonal Jordan evaluations, and its exact Sylvester block solves.

[F1] Success requires exact identities $Q^*Q=I$ and $A=QTQ^*$, diagonal blocks
$F_{ii}=f(T_{ii})$, and the block Parlett Sylvester equations
([[alg-schur-parlett-matrix-function]]).

[F2] The analytic primary function is a polynomial in its matrix, commutes
with it, and preserves block upper triangular form with diagonal blocks
$f(T_{ii})$
([[thm-analytic-primary-matrix-function-jordan-contour-agreement]]).

[F3] Every successful Bartels–Stewart solve has a unique exact solution because its verified local pivot maps are invertible and its finite block traversal solves the full operator ([[thm-bartels-stewart-finite-status-and-local-pivot-uniqueness]]).

[F4] A successful Bartels–Stewart substitution returns the exact local
Sylvester solution ([[thm-bartels-stewart-sylvester-exact-correctness]]).

## Proof

1.1 Let $G=f(T)$. By [F2], $G$ is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks $G_{ii}=f(T_{ii})$. By [F1], the algorithm's diagonal blocks equal these blocks. [F1, F2]

1.2 Expanding $GT=TG$ in block $(i,j)$ for $i<j$ gives $T_{ii}G_{ij}-G_{ij}T_{jj} =G_{ii}T_{ij}-T_{ij}G_{jj} +\sum_{i<k<j}(G_{ik}T_{kj}-T_{ik}G_{kj}).$ This is the recurrence solved by the algorithm. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Induct on the block distance $j-i$. At distance one, the recurrence right-hand side in step 1.2 uses only the matching diagonal blocks from step 1.1. The successful local solve from [F4] returns its exact solution, which is unique by the successful-pivot conclusion [F3]; hence $F_{ij}=G_{ij}$. At larger distance, all shorter blocks on the right-hand side already agree by induction, so the same uniqueness argument gives $F_{ij}=G_{ij}$. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, induction]

3.1 Steps 1.1 and 2.1 show $F=G=f(T)$. By [F1], $A=QTQ^*$ with $Q$ unitary; similarity invariance in [F2] gives $QFQ^*=Qf(T)Q^*=f(A)$, which is the returned factored value. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

      url: https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2013/file/ac1dd209cbcc5e5d1c6e28598e8cbbe8-Paper.pdf
      locator: Sections 2–3, Figure 1 and Theorem 1.
    - title: "Sébastien Bubeck, Convex Optimization: Algorithms and Complexity, complete monograph"
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1405.4980
      locator: Section 6.3, SVRG estimator, Lemma 6.4 and Theorem 6.5.
    - title: "Léon Bottou, Frank E. Curtis, and Jorge Nocedal, Optimization Methods for Large-Scale Machine Learning, SIAM Review 60(2) (2018)"
      url: https://leon.bottou.org/publications/pdf/tr-optml-2016.pdf
      locator: Section 5.3.1, Algorithm 5.1 and its gradient-work discussion.

## Definition

Let n,d>=1 and let f_1,...,f_n:R^d->R be continuously differentiable convex functions. Define the finite-sum objective

$$
F(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x),\qquad \nabla F(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\nabla f_i(x),
$$

where the gradient identity follows from [[lem-finite-sum-gradient-is-average]] and the sums use [[def-finite-sum]]. Suppose each component gradient is L-Lipschitz for a common L>0. An SVRG epoch with snapshot \tilde x and inner length m>=1 is:

1. Compute the full gradient \nabla F(\tilde x), set x_0=\tilde x.
2. For t=0,...,m-1, draw I_t uniformly from {1,...,n}, independently of the past, and set
   $$
   v_t=\nabla f_{I_t}(x_t)-\nabla f_{I_t}(\tilde x)+\nabla F(\tilde x),\qquad x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta v_t
   $$
   for a selected step size \eta>0.
3. Independently draw J uniformly from {0,...,m-1} and return x_J as the next snapshot.

The displayed procedure evaluates the snapshot component gradient at every inner update rather than caching those values. Its correction has the control-variate form of [[def-control-variate-estimator]] with coefficient one and the known finite-sum reference mean; the conditional properties needed here are proved in local results on this page. Conditional-expectation notation inherits the [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption from [[def-stochastic-gradient-oracle-and-unconstrained-update]].

## Statement

Let $d\ge2$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $V\in C^4(U,\mathbb R)$ using the convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Fix $x\in U$. Put $H=\nabla^2V(x)$ and suppose a validated ordered eigenvalue enclosure certifies index one with gap $\gamma>0$ as in [[def-validated-eigenvalue-enclosures-for-an-index-one-hessian]], so $\lambda_1(H)\le-\gamma$ and $\lambda_j(H)\ge\gamma$ for $j\ge2$. Let $\epsilon>0$, let $v$ be a unit direction accepted by the rotation test of [[alg-finite-budget-dimer-mode-following]], and assume the whole segment $x+[-\epsilon,\epsilon]v$ lies in $U$. Let $D_\epsilon$ be the paired-force estimate, with $\|(I-vv^T)D_\epsilon\|_2\le\tau_{\rm rot}$. Suppose each force evaluation has Euclidean error at most $\eta$ and the third derivatives of each gradient coordinate along this segment are bounded by $M_4$. Set

$$\delta:=\frac{\sqrt d\,M_4}{6}\epsilon^2+\frac{\eta}{\epsilon}.$$

If $\delta\le\gamma/4$ and the measured Rayleigh estimate $v^TD_\epsilon\le-\gamma/2$, then the sine of the angle from $v$ to the lowest-eigenvalue line of $H$ satisfies

$$\sin\angle(v,q_1):=\sqrt{1-|q_1^Tv|^2}\le\frac{4(\tau_{\rm rot}+\delta)}{5\gamma},$$

where $q_1$ is any unit eigenvector for $\lambda_1(H)$. This is a conditional mode bound; rotation success alone is not an index certificate.

Let $\epsilon_g=\|\nabla V(x)\|_2$. If $\epsilon_g=0$, $x$ itself is an index-one critical point. If $\epsilon_g>0$, put $\rho=2\epsilon_g/\gamma$ and additionally assume $B_2(x,2\rho)\subset U$, $H(\cdot)=\nabla^2V(\cdot)$ is $L$-Lipschitz on that ball, and $L\rho/\gamma\le1/2$. Then there is a unique index-one critical point $x_*$ in $\overline B_2(x,\rho)$ and

$$\|x_*-x\|_2\le\rho=\frac{2\epsilon_g}{\gamma}.$$

The dimer direction bound does not replace the validated eigenvalue enclosure or the residual, inverse, and Hessian-Lipschitz conditions in this local saddle certificate.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The potential and point, validated ordered eigenvalue enclosure, accepted unit dimer direction, paired-force estimate and error data, gradient residual, and (when $\epsilon_g>0$) the local Hessian-Lipschitz hypotheses in the Statement.

[A1] The validated intervals establish $\lambda_1(H)\le-\gamma$ and $\lambda_j(H)\ge\gamma$ for $j\ge2$ ([[def-validated-eigenvalue-enclosures-for-an-index-one-hessian]]).

[A2] The dimer rotation test has accepted $v$ with $\|(I-vv^T)D_\epsilon\|_2\le\tau_{\rm rot}$, and $v^TD_\epsilon\le-\gamma/2$.

[A3] The force errors and third-derivative bound give the stated value $\delta$.

[A4] For the local saddle conclusion with $\epsilon_g>0$, the stated ball, Hessian-Lipschitz, and radius hypotheses hold.

[F1] Since $V\in C^4$, it is $C^2$; [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]] makes $H$ symmetric, hence self-adjoint in the standard Euclidean inner product, so [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis.

[F2] [[lem-dimer-central-force-hessian-vector-error]]: $\|D_\epsilon-Hv\|_2\le\delta$ under the stated paired-force and derivative-error bounds.

[F3] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: for a unit vector $v$, $|v^Tw|\le\|w\|_2$; orthogonal projection $I-vv^T$ does not increase Euclidean norm, by the orthogonal decomposition into parallel and perpendicular parts.

[F4] [[thm-local-index-one-saddle-certificate-from-enclosures]]: the eigenvalue gap, gradient residual, inverse bound, and local Hessian-Lipschitz/radius conditions give the stated unique nearby index-one critical point.



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [F1], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $q_1,\ldots,q_d$ for $H$, ordered so that their eigenvalues are $\lambda_1\le\cdots\le\lambda_d$. Since $v$ is unit, write $v=\sum_{j=1}^d c_jq_j$ with $\sum_jc_j^2=1$. [A1, F1, given]

2.1 Put $\mu=v^THv$. From [F2] and [F3], $|v^T(D_\epsilon-Hv)|\le\delta$, so $\mu\le v^TD_\epsilon+\delta\le-\gamma/2+\gamma/4=-\gamma/4$. [A2, A3, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since $v^THv=\mu$, $(I-vv^T)Hv=(H-\mu I)v$. By [A2], [F2], and the projection bound in [F3], $\|(H-\mu I)v\|_2\le\|(I-vv^T)D_\epsilon\|_2+\|(I-vv^T)(Hv-D_\epsilon)\|_2\le\tau_{\rm rot}+\delta$. [A2, A3, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For every $j\ge2$, [A1] and step 2.1 give $\lambda_j-\mu\ge\gamma+\gamma/4=5\gamma/4$. Expanding step 3.1 in the eigenbasis from step 1.1 yields $\left(\frac{5\gamma}{4}\right)^2\sum_{j=2}^dc_j^2\le\sum_{j=2}^d(\lambda_j-\mu)^2c_j^2\le\|(H-\mu I)v\|_2^2\le(\tau_{\rm rot}+\delta)^2$. As $\sum_{j=2}^dc_j^2=1-|q_1^Tv|^2$, taking nonnegative square roots proves the stated sine-angle bound. [A1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 If $\epsilon_g=0$, the zero-residual branch of [[thm-local-index-one-saddle-certificate-from-enclosures]] and [A1] make $x$ an exact index-one critical point. If $\epsilon_g>0$, [A1] and [A4] are exactly the enclosure, residual, and neighborhood hypotheses of [F4]; applying it gives the unique index-one critical point in the radius-$\rho$ ball and the bound $\|x_*-x\|_2\le2\epsilon_g/\gamma$. This local error conclusion is independent of the mode-angle estimate and adds no global convergence claim for the finite dimer iteration. [A1, A4, F4, step 4.1, given] ∎

## Statement

Let $d\ge2$, let $V\in C^4(U,\mathbb R)$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, and let $x\in U$. Put $H=\nabla^2V(x)$ and $\epsilon_g=\|\nabla V(x)\|_2$. Suppose a validated ordered eigenvalue enclosure certifies index one with gap $\gamma>0$ in the sense of [[def-validated-eigenvalue-enclosures-for-an-index-one-hessian]]. If $\epsilon_g=0$, then $x$ is an exact critical point with Hessian index one.

If $\epsilon_g>0$, put $\rho=2\epsilon_g/\gamma$. Assume $B_2(x,2\rho)\subset U$, the Hessian is $L$-Lipschitz in the induced Euclidean operator norm there, and $L\rho/\gamma\le1/2$. Then there is exactly one critical point $x_*$ in $\overline B_2(x,\rho)$, it satisfies $\|x_*-x\|_2\le\rho$, and its Hessian has exactly one negative eigenvalue and no zero eigenvalues. The reported residual $\epsilon_g$, gap $\gamma$, conditioning bound $1/\gamma$, Hessian Lipschitz constant $L$, and radius condition are part of the certificate; a residual or a Ritz value alone is not a certificate.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The potential, point, gradient residual, interval evidence, gap, and local Hessian-Lipschitz hypotheses in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-validated-eigenvalue-enclosures-for-an-index-one-hessian]]: the validated intervals certify $\lambda_1(H)\le-\gamma$ and $\lambda_j(H)\ge\gamma$ for $j\ge2$.

[F2] Since $V\in C^4$, it is $C^2$, and [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]] gives $H^T=H$. In the standard Euclidean inner product this is a self-adjoint endomorphism, so [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis.

[F3] [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]] and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] define $H$ and the gradient. [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] identifies the matrix of $D(\nabla V)$ with the gradient Jacobian; [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]] makes its entries agree with the Hessian convention. A critical point is a zero of the gradient.

[F4] [[lem-local-root-from-uniformly-small-residual]]: if $DF(x)$ is invertible, has inverse norm at most $\beta$, and is $L$-Lipschitz on a sufficiently large ball, then $\|F(x)\|$ small enough gives a unique nearby zero within $2\beta\|F(x)\|$.

[F5] [[thm-courant-fischer-min-max-principle]]: the largest eigenvalue is the maximum Rayleigh quotient, and the second largest is at most the maximum Rayleigh quotient on the orthogonal complement of a leading eigenvector.

[F6] [[thm-operator-norm-is-the-largest-singular-value]]: the maximum defining the finite-dimensional Euclidean operator norm exists, and its definition bounds $\|Bw\|_2$ by $\|B\|_{\rm op}\|w\|_2$.

[F7] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: $|u^Tw|\le\|u\|_2\|w\|_2$.



**Given:** The data in the Statement.

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], the eigenvalues of $H$ are all at least distance $\gamma$ from zero. Using the orthonormal eigenbasis in [F2], $H$ is invertible and each unit vector is expanded by $H^{-1}$ by at most $1/\gamma$; [F6] therefore gives $\|H^{-1}\|_{\rm op}\le1/\gamma$. [F1, F2, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 If $\epsilon_g=0$, [F3] says $x$ is critical, and [F1] says its Hessian has exactly one negative eigenvalue. Suppose henceforth $\epsilon_g>0$ and use the inverse bound $\beta=1/\gamma$ from step 1.1. The radius in [F4] is then exactly $2\beta\epsilon_g=\rho$, and its Lipschitz condition is $\beta L\rho=L\rho/\gamma\le1/2$. Since $B_2(x,2\rho)\subset U$, every hypothesis of [F4] holds on the stated ball, so there is exactly one zero $x_*$ of $\nabla V$ in $\overline B_2(x,\rho)$ and $\|x_*-x\|_2\le\rho$. [F1, F3, F4, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Set $A=-H(x)$ and $E=-(H(x_*)-H(x))$. Then $A$ is symmetric with largest eigenvalue at least $\gamma$ and second-largest at most $-\gamma$. The Lipschitz hypothesis is in the induced Euclidean operator norm, so $\|E\|_{\rm op}\le L\rho\le\gamma/2$ by step 2.1. [F1, F2, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 Let $q_1$ be a unit leading eigenvector of $A$. The maximum Rayleigh formula in [F5] yields $\lambda_1(A+E)\ge q_1^T(A+E)q_1\ge\lambda_1(A)-\|E\|_{\rm op}\ge\gamma/2>0$ by [F6, F7]. The second-eigenvalue min-max formula in [F5], applied to $q_1^\perp$, yields $\lambda_2(A+E)\le\lambda_2(A)+\|E\|_{\rm op}\le-\gamma/2<0$. Every later eigenvalue is at most the second, so $A+E=-H(x_*)$ has exactly one positive eigenvalue and no zero eigenvalue. Thus $H(x_*)$ has exactly one negative eigenvalue and no zero eigenvalues. Together with step 2.1 this proves the stated local certificate; if $\epsilon_g=0$, step 2.1 already proved it. [F1, F2, F5, F6, F7, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
